at.step: The same bin-packing question comes in three shapes: decision asks only yes or no, search asks for an actual packing, and optimization asks for the fewest bins possible. The theory is built on the decision form, because yes or no is the simplest answer to compare and to build reductions out of.

Walking that self-reduction on a real graph: one call confirms a witness of the target size exists, then each vertex is tried for removal in turn. A vertex whose removal keeps the answer yes gets dropped for good; a vertex whose removal flips the answer to no stays, and belongs in the final set.

A decision problem answers only yes or no. P is every decision problem some procedure solves in time bounded by a fixed power of the input's length. NP is every decision problem where a yes answer comes with a proof — a certificate — that a separate procedure can check in that same bounded time: a verifier.

Every problem in P is already in NP, because solving it from scratch is itself a valid proof. Whether that containment runs the other way is the open question behind the field's most famous unanswered prize. The letters themselves name a kind of machine, not the word 'not': nondeterministic polynomial time.

syllabus.clause: Karp reductions and their direction (reduce from the known-hard problem)

at.step: A Karp reduction from problem A to problem B is a function, computable quickly, that maps every yes-instance of A to a yes-instance of B and every no-instance to a no-instance. To show B is at least as hard as A, the function has to run from the already-known-hard problem toward the new one, never the other way.

One reduction, checked completely rather than merely argued: map a graph and a target size to the same graph and the vertex count minus that size. A set is independent exactly when its complement covers every edge, so the map sends every yes-instance to a yes-instance and every no-instance to a no-instance, confirmed on every small graph there is.

That mistaken direction is not just unhelpful, it is vacuous: every problem solvable quickly reduces to almost any other problem at all, by solving the easy one first and then outputting one of two fixed, already-decided instances of the target. A reduction built this way carries no information about the target whatsoever.
